PROPOSITION 3
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by
Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional
Amendment.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It
pays for most spending from the state’s main operating account, the General Fund. The General
Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health
care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and
profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out
low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple
pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000
and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily
increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to
extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher
rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion
from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for
schools, community colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a
minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state
spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health
insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 3
PROPOSAL
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent
instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this
measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount
of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is
because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market,
which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in
revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the
state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education
and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community
colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in
budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 3 of 3

A YES vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place
since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
A NO vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place
since 2012 would expire in 2031.

ers.

If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last.

Prop. 3 would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031.

“I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.”

Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners. 

Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3%, the highest in the nation.

The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. 

Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges.

In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said.

Union’s big push

The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.”

The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500.

The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes on the measure. Among Democrats, 82% said they favored it, while 18% of Republicans said they did.

Prop. 3 is not the only tax-the-rich measure on the Nov. 3 ballot. Proposition 40 would levy a 5% tax on Californians with assets of more than $1 billion, with 90% of the money going toward healthcare and the rest divided between schools, food assistance programs and other services. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said. 

“We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said.

The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said.

‘Not sustainable’

Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments and declining enrollment. 

“We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.”

In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes. 

California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living.

Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11.

That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now. 

“Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.”

He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding.

“No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said.

If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last.

Prop. 3 would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031.

“I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.”

Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners. 

Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3%, the highest in the nation.

The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. 

Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges.

In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said.

Union’s big push

The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.”

The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500.

The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes on the measure. Among Democrats, 82% said they favored it, while 18% of Republicans said they did.

Prop. 3 is not the only tax-the-rich measure on the Nov. 3 ballot. Proposition 40 would levy a 5% tax on Californians with assets of more than $1 billion, with 90% of the money going toward healthcare and the rest divided between schools, food assistance programs and other services. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said. 

“We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said.

The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said.

‘Not sustainable’

Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments and declining enrollment. 

“We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.”

In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes. 

California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living.

Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11.

That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now. 

“Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.”

He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding.

“No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said.

These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 through 2030.
Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent.
Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets.
The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.

(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 3 would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue that would otherwise disappear when the higher income tax rates expire after 2030.
The amount collected would vary from year to year because earnings among high-income taxpayers are especially sensitive to changes in the economy and stock market.
Roughly 40 percent of the additional revenue would support K–12 schools and community colleges, while most of the remainder would be available for other General Fund programs and state reserves.

content.text:
ers.

If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last.

Prop. 3 would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031.

“I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.”

Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners. 

Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3%, the highest in the nation.

The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. 

Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges.

In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said.

Union’s big push

The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.”

The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500.

The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes on the measure. Among Democrats, 82% said they favored it, while 18% of Republicans said they did.

Prop. 3 is not the only tax-the-rich measure on the Nov. 3 ballot. Proposition 40 would levy a 5% tax on Californians with assets of more than $1 billion, with 90% of the money going toward healthcare and the rest divided between schools, food assistance programs and other services. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said. 

“We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said.

The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said.

‘Not sustainable’

Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments and declining enrollment. 

“We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.”

In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes. 

California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living.

Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11.

That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now. 

“Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.”

He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding.

“No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said.

If rejected, tax rates for the top 2% would fall in 2031 from at least 10.3% to 9.3%.
How much they have raised
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text">
Fundraising data will be updated regularly until the election.
What does the tax fund?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Then, because the state constitution requires minimum levels of spending on education, more dollars are freed up to pay for services including healthcare and the University of California and California State University systems, said Kayla Kitson, a senior analyst with the California Budget and Policy Center.
Proposition 3, like the current high-earners tax, has the added effect of raising the minimum levels of funding required to flow to K-12 schools and community colleges, because of the complicated formulas California uses to set its budget, Kitson said.
If Proposition 3 fails, the state could expect to lose between $5 billion and $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Advertisement
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Supporters of the measure include the California Teachers Assn., the California School Nurses Organization, the California State PTA and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California.
The California Teachers Assn., whose members gathered signatures to put Proposition 3 on the ballot, says if voters reject the measure, public schools could face a 15% budget cut, with 1 in 6 educators at risk of losing their jobs.
“Prop. 3 keeps the wealthiest Californians paying their share so our public schools get the funding our students deserve,” the union says on its website (https://www.cta.org/educator/posts/yes-on-prop3).
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The California Taxpayers Assn., the Family Business Assn. of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce have come out against the measure.
Opponents say the state already has the nation’s highest income, sales and gas taxes and Sacramento needs to stop wasteful spending, rather than make taxes that were supposed to be temporary permanent.
Advertisement
“Californians shouldn’t have to bail out politicians and special interests’ mismanagement,” an opposition website sponsored by the California Taxpayers Assn. says. “Waste, fraud and overspending by the state government is not an excuse to raise our taxes even higher.”

Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Provides Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care By Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
High-Income Tax, Renew State Income Tax Increase for Education Funding Initiative
The California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering. 874,641 valid signatures were required. The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents. These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-6-2012-general-election-summary/november-6) in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-8-2016-general-election-summary/november-8-2) through 2030. Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent. Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets. The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 3 would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue that would otherwise disappear when the higher income tax rates expire after 2030. The amount collected would vary from year to year because earnings among high-income taxpayers are especially sensitive to changes in the economy and stock market. Roughly 40 percent of the additional revenue would support K–12 schools and community colleges, while most of the remainder would be available for other General Fund programs and state reserves.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote would permanently continue California’s higher income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% on high-income earners, with the resulting education funding divided between K–12 schools (89%) and community colleges (11%).
NO: A “no” vote would leave current law unchanged, allowing these higher tax rates to expire in 2031.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents of Proposition 3 believe that the continuation of higher tax requirements on high-income earners is a crucial investment in students, communities, and educators. They maintain that the general population are demonstrably angry about income inequality and that failure to pass the proposition amounts to a tax cut for wealthy Californians.
Opponents argue that permanently extending the higher rates could encourage wealthy residents and businesses to leave California, potentially affecting jobs and economic growth. They also contend that making the rates permanent would make the policy harder to change in the future.

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 3 stems from a decision voters made in 2012, amid a budget crisis, to temporarily increase the income tax rate on the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030.
Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
If passed, tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers.
Advertisement
If rejected, tax rates for the top 2% would fall in 2031 from at least 10.3% to 9.3%.
How much they have raised
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text">
Fundraising data will be updated regularly until the election.
What does the tax fund?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Then, because the state constitution requires minimum levels of spending on education, more dollars are freed up to pay for services including healthcare and the University of California and California State University systems, said Kayla Kitson, a senior analyst with the California Budget and Policy Center.
Proposition 3, like the current high-earners tax, has the added effect of raising the minimum levels of funding required to flow to K-12 schools and community colleges, because of the complicated formulas California uses to set its budget, Kitson said.
If Proposition 3 fails, the state could expect to lose between $5 billion and $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Advertisement
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Supporters of the measure include the California Teachers Assn., the California School Nurses Organization, the California State PTA and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California.
The California Teachers Assn., whose members gathered signatures to put Proposition 3 on the ballot, says if voters reject the measure, public schools could face a 15% budget cut, with 1 in 6 educators at risk of losing their jobs.
“Prop. 3 keeps the wealthiest Californians paying their share so our public schools get the funding our students deserve,” the union says on its website (https://www.cta.org/educator/posts/yes-on-prop3).
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The California Taxpayers Assn., the Family Business Assn. of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce have come out against the measure.
Opponents say the state already has the nation’s highest income, sales and gas taxes and Sacramento needs to stop wasteful spending, rather than make taxes that were supposed to be temporary permanent.
Advertisement
“Californians shouldn’t have to bail out politicians and special interests’ mismanagement,” an opposition website sponsored by the California Taxpayers Assn. says. “Waste, fraud and overspending by the state government is not an excuse to raise our taxes even higher.”

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 3 stems from a decision voters made in 2012, amid a budget crisis, to temporarily increase the income tax rate on the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030.
Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
If passed, tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers.
Advertisement
If rejected, tax rates for the top 2% would fall in 2031 from at least 10.3% to 9.3%.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text">
Fundraising data will be updated regularly until the election.
What does the tax fund?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Then, because the state constitution requires minimum levels of spending on education, more dollars are freed up to pay for services including healthcare and the University of California and California State University systems, said Kayla Kitson, a senior analyst with the California Budget and Policy Center.
Proposition 3, like the current high-earners tax, has the added effect of raising the minimum levels of funding required to flow to K-12 schools and community colleges, because of the complicated formulas California uses to set its budget, Kitson said.
If Proposition 3 fails, the state could expect to lose between $5 billion and $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Advertisement
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Supporters of the measure include the California Teachers Assn., the California School Nurses Organization, the California State PTA and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California.
The California Teachers Assn., whose members gathered signatures to put Proposition 3 on the ballot, says if voters reject the measure, public schools could face a 15% budget cut, with 1 in 6 educators at risk of losing their jobs.
“Prop. 3 keeps the wealthiest Californians paying their share so our public schools get the funding our students deserve,” the union says on its website (https://www.cta.org/educator/posts/yes-on-prop3).
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The California Taxpayers Assn., the Family Business Assn. of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce have come out against the measure.
Opponents say the state already has the nation’s highest income, sales and gas taxes and Sacramento needs to stop wasteful spending, rather than make taxes that were supposed to be temporary permanent.
Advertisement
“Californians shouldn’t have to bail out politicians and special interests’ mismanagement,” an opposition website sponsored by the California Taxpayers Assn. says. “Waste, fraud and overspending by the state government is not an excuse to raise our taxes even higher.”

Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Provides Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care By Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
High-Income Tax, Renew State Income Tax Increase for Education Funding Initiative
The California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering. 874,641 valid signatures were required. The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents. These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-6-2012-general-election-summary/november-6) in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-8-2016-general-election-summary/november-8-2) through 2030. Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent. Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets. The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 3 would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue that would otherwise disappear when the higher income tax rates expire after 2030. The amount collected would vary from year to year because earnings among high-income taxpayers are especially sensitive to changes in the economy and stock market. Roughly 40 percent of the additional revenue would support K–12 schools and community colleges, while most of the remainder would be available for other General Fund programs and state reserves.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote would permanently continue California’s higher income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% on high-income earners, with the resulting education funding divided between K–12 schools (89%) and community colleges (11%).
NO: A “no” vote would leave current law unchanged, allowing these higher tax rates to expire in 2031.

Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Provides Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care By Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
High-Income Tax, Renew State Income Tax Increase for Education Funding Initiative
The California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering. 874,641 valid signatures were required. The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents. These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-6-2012-general-election-summary/november-6) in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-8-2016-general-election-summary/november-8-2) through 2030. Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent. Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets. The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 3 would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue that would otherwise disappear when the higher income tax rates expire after 2030. The amount collected would vary from year to year because earnings among high-income taxpayers are especially sensitive to changes in the economy and stock market. Roughly 40 percent of the additional revenue would support K–12 schools and community colleges, while most of the remainder would be available for other General Fund programs and state reserves.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote would permanently continue California’s higher income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% on high-income earners, with the resulting education funding divided between K–12 schools (89%) and community colleges (11%).
NO: A “no” vote would leave current law unchanged, allowing these higher tax rates to expire in 2031.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 3 would make an expiring state income tax on high earners permanent, which supporters say is critical to funding schools and healthcare.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
California’s general election takes place on Novemer 3. Learn about L.A.’s city and county races as well races for state office.
Oct. 1, 2026
What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 3 stems from a decision voters made in 2012, amid a budget crisis, to temporarily increase the income tax rate on the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030.
Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
If passed, tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers.
Advertisement
If rejected, tax rates for the top 2% would fall in 2031 from at least 10.3% to 9.3%.
How much they have raised
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text">
Fundraising data will be updated regularly until the election.
What does the tax fund?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Then, because the state constitution requires minimum levels of spending on education, more dollars are freed up to pay for services including healthcare and the University of California and California State University systems, said Kayla Kitson, a senior analyst with the California Budget and Policy Center.
Proposition 3, like the current high-earners tax, has the added effect of raising the minimum levels of funding required to flow to K-12 schools and community colleges, because of the complicated formulas California uses to set its budget, Kitson said.
If Proposition 3 fails, the state could expect to lose between $5 billion and $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Advertisement
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Supporters of the measure include the California Teachers Assn., the California School Nurses Organization, the California State PTA and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California.
The California Teachers Assn., whose members gathered signatures to put Proposition 3 on the ballot, says if voters reject the measure, public schools could face a 15% budget cut, with 1 in 6 educators at risk of losing their jobs.
“Prop. 3 keeps the wealthiest Californians paying their share so our public schools get the funding our students deserve,” the union says on its website (https://www.cta.org/educator/posts/yes-on-prop3).
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The California Taxpayers Assn., the Family Business Assn. of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce have come out against the measure.
Opponents say the state already has the nation’s highest income, sales and gas taxes and Sacramento needs to stop wasteful spending, rather than make taxes that were supposed to be temporary permanent.
Advertisement
“Californians shouldn’t have to bail out politicians and special interests’ mismanagement,” an opposition website sponsored by the California Taxpayers Assn. says. “Waste, fraud and overspending by the state government is not an excuse to raise our taxes even higher.”

Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Provides Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care By Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
High-Income Tax, Renew State Income Tax Increase for Education Funding Initiative
The California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering. 874,641 valid signatures were required. The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents. These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-6-2012-general-election-summary/november-6) in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-8-2016-general-election-summary/november-8-2) through 2030. Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent. Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets. The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 3 would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue that would otherwise disappear when the higher income tax rates expire after 2030. The amount collected would vary from year to year because earnings among high-income taxpayers are especially sensitive to changes in the economy and stock market. Roughly 40 percent of the additional revenue would support K–12 schools and community colleges, while most of the remainder would be available for other General Fund programs and state reserves.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote would permanently continue California’s higher income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% on high-income earners, with the resulting education funding divided between K–12 schools (89%) and community colleges (11%).
NO: A “no” vote would leave current law unchanged, allowing these higher tax rates to expire in 2031.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents of Proposition 3 believe that the continuation of higher tax requirements on high-income earners is a crucial investment in students, communities, and educators. They maintain that the general population are demonstrably angry about income inequality and that failure to pass the proposition amounts to a tax cut for wealthy Californians.
Opponents argue that permanently extending the higher rates could encourage wealthy residents and businesses to leave California, potentially affecting jobs and economic growth. They also contend that making the rates permanent would make the policy harder to change in the future.

Proposition 3
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for most spending from the state's main operating account, the General Fund. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000 and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
Proposal
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
Fiscal Effects
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market, which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
A NO vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact : Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031.

Next I'm looking at the opponents' main claims, like the "largest permanent tax increase" and the 13.3% top rate, to see which parts are factual and which are framing.

I'm checking the opponents' budget claims now, starting with the "$100B surplus turned into a $30B deficit" line. I want to test it against the LAO's outlook, since the surplus figure and the later deficits are the parts I need to pin down.

I'm checking the Yes side's "billions in cuts" line against the LAO's $5 to 15 billion revenue estimate, since a revenue loss doesn't automatically mean cuts. Prop 98 ties school funding to General Fund revenue, so a loss would lower the school guarantee by roughly 40% of the shortfall, which is the part I need to pin down.

I'm working out whether the Prop 98 guarantee would shrink by roughly 40% of any lost revenue, which would put a $5–15 billion revenue loss at about $2–6 billion less for schools. I'm also checking whether the "50,000 teachers" figure from the opposing side is plausible given that amount, though I don't need to settle it. Next I want to look at research on how high-income tax changes have affected migration in California.

I'm checking whether tax increases on high earners really drive out wealthy taxpayers, since that bears on whether the revenue projections hold up. I'll look for research on California migration and see whether the LAO's analysis addresses behavioral responses.

I'm checking how the LAO's analysis treats high earners who might move or shift income in response to the tax, since that affects how stable the revenue is. I'm also looking at the constitutional amendment's permanence: changing it later would take voter approval, which is the opponents' core objection.

I'm checking whether the measure makes the rates permanent by amending the Constitution, since that would mean future legislatures couldn't lower them without voters. I'll look at the LAO's full text to see whether it spells that out, and whether the Section 36 amendment or the statutory Revenue and Taxation Code rates are what actually controls.

I'm checking whether the Prop 3 rates would be locked into the Constitution, since the tax brackets currently sit in Section 36 of Article XIII and the statute they reference. Changing them later would take a constitutional amendment, which means voter approval, and that's the "harder to change" point I want to confirm in the LAO's full analysis.

I'm also going to check Ballotpedia for a summary that covers the arguments and campaign contributions, and I'll look at the Yes and No campaign sites and the Secretary of State's contributions page in parallel.

Proposition 3
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for most spending from the state's main operating account, the General Fund. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000 and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
Proposal
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
Fiscal Effects
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market, which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
A NO vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031.

Story Title:
Proposition 3: California doesn’t need another forever tax
October 28, 2026
Download featured image (https://edsource.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/voting10.jpg)
This story was originally published by EdSource (https://edsource.org/2026/commentary-vote-no-proposition-3/769223). Sign up for their daily newsletter (https://edsource.org/subscribe).
Proposition 3 asks voters to approve a massive tax increase that would not take effect until 2031, when California’s finances may look completely different from how they do today. Voters should reject Proposition 3 and keep their options open.
In 2031, there will be a new president in the Oval Office, a new governor, and a different political landscape in California — especially if voters approve Proposition 40 to impose a wealth tax that could prompt an exodus of the taxpayers targeted by Proposition 3.
Related Reading
CommentaryProposition 3 would help lock in hard-won resources for student well-being (https://edsource.org/2026/proposition-3-california-schools/769155) October 28, 2026
The state also will have significantly fewer students in our public schools. The Department of Finance projects a decline of 710,500 students from 2026 through 2036, and by the midpoint of this decline, we undoubtedly will see some major changes in the education structure.
This is only the beginning of the list of unknowns. Other questions include:
Will Californians still be paying billions of dollars per year for a nonfunctioning “high-speed” railroad system in 2031, rather than prioritizing schools for that spending?
Will taxpayers still be paying for ineffective programs that haven’t solved homelessness?
Will startups launch in California, or take their jobs and economic benefits to states with more competitive tax rates?
In short, it makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
What difference could five years make?
California’s finances can change substantially in a short period. Total state revenue for the current fiscal year is projected to be $21.5 billion higher than the amount collected five years earlier. The Department of Finance also recently reported that general fund revenue was running $5.5 billion above the projection used to draft the 2026-27 budget just six months earlier. This means the education funding guarantee will go up, too.
It makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
Timing is only one of the problems. While Proposition 3 is marketed as a “tax extension” that would only affect high-income residents, the truth is that it’s a major tax increase that would hit millions of small businesses as well as high-income individuals. The result: California’s affordability crisis gets worse.
The small-business aspect of Proposition 3 hasn’t received enough attention. California’s tax structure does not neatly separate business income from personal income, and many small businesses operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships, or S corporations that report business earnings on personal income tax returns.
This means the higher tax rates imposed by Proposition 3 would increase taxes on many small businesses, ultimately leading to higher prices for customers, fewer job opportunities for workers, or both.
ThePublic Policy Institute of California reported in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-businesses/) that sole proprietorships accounted for more than 3 million California businesses in 2023. But the number of those businesses whose owners would be impacted by Proposition 3 depends on their taxable income.
To the extent that Proposition 3 would hit high-income earners, it would make California more reliant on the most volatile source of revenue, while simultaneously making it even more volatile by giving high-income residents a new incentive to leave the state.
California already imposes the nation’s highest personal income taxes and would have a top personal income tax rate of 10.3% on income over $1 million without Proposition 3. The state also imposes a 1.3% State Disability Insurance tax on all income from salaries and wages, bringing the top tax rate to 11.6% on those forms of income, without Proposition 3.
As for the issue of an “extension” versus an “increase,” the fact is clear: If Proposition 3 is approved, Californians will pay $5 billion to $15 billion a year more in state income tax than if the initiative is defeated (according to estimates by the Legislative Analyst’s Office). That’s an increase — and a very large one, at that.
Finally, the measure would continue the trend in which “temporary” taxes in California never seem to go away. As the proponents of Proposition 40 are discovering, voters are extremely distrustful of taxes described as temporary. Why? In large part because of Proposition 3 and its predecessor, Proposition 55 of 2016, asking voters to renew a tax originally described as a temporary charge to cover an emergency.
The ballot argument for the original initiative, Proposition 30 of 2012, said the taxes “are temporary, balanced and necessary to protect schools and safety” — one of the argument’s five mentions of the allegedly temporary nature.
With revenue arriving above projections and the state spending billions on questionable programs without proper controls or a review of effectiveness, it can no longer be said that California has a fiscal emergency.
The voters should give much-needed relief to small businesses and their customers, avoid making fiscal decisions prematurely, and let the “emergency tax” expire on schedule. Vote NO on Proposition 3.
•••
Robert Gutierrez is president of the California Taxpayers Association (https://caltax.org/), which is celebrating its 100th year of serving as the state’s largest and oldest association representing taxpayers in this state.

Prop
3
CA
Prop
3
|
Constitutional Amendment
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes
Makes permanent the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners to fund education, healthcare, and other state programs.
SPUR's Recommendation
Prop. 3 would make permanent an existing high-earner tax that funds K–12/community college education, children’s healthcare, and debt paydown. This tax has generated more than $119 billion for education and healthcare, with no evidence that it has driven high earners out of state. It’s highly progressive, hitting only top earners while sustaining programs such as universal school meals that disproportionately benefit low-income students, and it would help backfill Medi-Cal funding just as federal cuts threaten healthcare access for millions of low-income Californians. The trade-offs are modest: permanence would limit future tax flexibility, and reliance on capital-gains-linked income would keep revenue volatile. But given the tax's proven track record and the increasingly dramatic funding gaps the tax would help fill in the wake of H.R. 1, SPUR supports making it permanent.
Vote YES
What Prop. 3 Would Do
Proposition 3 would amend the California Constitution to permanently extend the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners, which have been in place since 2012 under Proposition 55 and are set to expire in 2030. In 2025, the top 2% income bracket started at $371,001 a year for individuals and $743,001 a year for couples filing jointly. The tax applies to salaries, wages, interest, and profits from stocks, property, and other investments.
Revenue would primarily support K–12 schools and community colleges under 1988’s Proposition 98. About 40% — $2 billion to $6 billion annually — would go to education, while remaining funds could support children’s healthcare, the Budget Stabilization Account (rainy day fund), and other General Fund uses. Because the revenue counts toward the state’s required education funding, it frees up General Fund dollars for other programs. 1
If the tax rates set in 2012 expire, the state would lose between $5 billion and $15 billion annually. 2 In the short term, the state would need other General Fund revenues to meet education funding requirements; over time, the Proposition 98-mandated spending minimum could decline depending on the formula in use, economic conditions, and legislative decisions.
The Backstory
California’s personal income tax structure is the most progressive in the country (meaning the tax rate is higher the more income one earns). Voters approved Prop. 30 in 2012 to temporarily raise rates on high earners, then extended it through Prop. 55 in 2016 (expiring in 2030). Before Prop. 30, the top rate was 9.3%.
The tax structure for the top 2% of earners in California under different scenarios depends on whether Prop. 3 passes.

Prop. 98 requires California to provide a minimum level of funding for K–12 schools and community colleges each year, based on state revenues, economic growth, and student enrollment. Local property taxes also contribute to the Prop. 98 minimum. Together, these requirements typically direct about 40% of General Fund revenues to education. 3
Of the education funding, 89% goes to K–12 schools and 11% to community colleges. None of the funding can be used for administrative costs. After meeting education requirements, revenues go to debt service and the rainy day fund; 50% of remaining funds, capped at $2 billion annually, may support Medi-Cal children’s and family health services.
Medi-Cal provides free or low-cost health care to nearly 15 million Californians. This funding is especially important after federal bill H.R. 1 made major cuts to health care and food assistance. Federal Medicaid cuts could cost Medi-Cal tens of billions of dollars annually and cause up to 2 million Californians to lose coverage.
Since January 1, 2012, the top-earner income tax has generated more than $119 billion for education and healthcare, helping more than double school funding and support transitional kindergarten, expanded learning, free school meals, COVID-19 recovery, and teacher recruitment. 4 Before the passage of Prop. 30, California ranked 50th among states in per-student education spending. Now it ranks 16th (or 31st when accounting for the state’s cost of living). 5 However, because 80% of school spending goes to staff salaries and benefits, the state still has 22 students per teacher, compared with 15.4 nationally. 6
Recently, the tax has generated about $9 billion to $10 billion annually, although revenues fluctuate with the economy and stock market. The LAO estimates annual revenues could range from $5 billion to $15 billion.
Notably, high earners have not fled the state because of this tax; California has had the second-lowest out-migration rate among $200,000-plus households of any state over the past decade. 7 The state has lost less-educated and lower-income adults faster than higher-income and college-educated adults because of affordability and cost-of-living concerns. 8
Californians for Protecting Public Education, Health Care and Budget Stability led the effort to put Proposition 3 on the ballot, with funding from the California Teachers Association and California Federation of Teachers. Some proponents oppose Prop. 40, the Billionaire Tax, out of concern that it could undermine support for Prop. 3.
A citizen-initiated measure, Prop. 3 needs a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Allowing the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners to expire would require major cuts to education spending on the next generation of Californians, which would disproportionately impact low-income children and students of color. This income tax revenue enabled California to become the first state offering free breakfast and lunch to all TK–12 students, plus free after-school programs prioritizing low-income neighborhoods.
California’s educational funding formula, the Local Control Funding Formula, directs the most resources to students who face the greatest educational hurdles, including grants for English learners, foster youth, homeless students, and low-income families in high-poverty districts. 9
Prop. 3 would backfill federal cuts and sustain up to $2 billion in annual funding for Medi-Cal, most of which goes to low-income people and people of color. Without state budget and policy intervention, the cuts from H.R. 1 are expected to completely destabilize California’s healthcare and hospital system, exacerbate food insecurity, and cause children to miss routine screenings and vaccines. 10
The measure is highly progressive; it does not increase taxes on couples earning less than $743,001 or individuals earning less than $341,001, in today’s dollars.
Pros
Prop. 3 would help backfill ongoing funding needs for children’s healthcare and Medi-Cal, which is facing severe federal funding cuts.
The measure would tax only California’s highest earners.
It would not increase the current income tax rate, which was set in 2012.
Any leftover capital-gains-driven revenue would lower state debt and help build the rainy day fund, which supports the state’s financial health and mitigates the volatility of this funding source.
There is no evidence that the tax has contributed to any significant tax flight from the state.
Because the tax is permanent, it would facilitate greater predictability in state revenues.
Cons
The state’s reliance on taxing the highest income earners would increase state budget volatility.
The measure is restrictive: it would require meeting the Prop. 98 education minimum before allowing flexibility in funding allocation.

Story Title:
Proposition 3: California doesn’t need another forever tax
October 28, 2026
Download featured image (https://edsource.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/voting10.jpg)
This story was originally published by EdSource (https://edsource.org/2026/commentary-vote-no-proposition-3/769223). Sign up for their daily newsletter (https://edsource.org/subscribe).
Proposition 3 asks voters to approve a massive tax increase that would not take effect until 2031, when California’s finances may look completely different from how they do today. Voters should reject Proposition 3 and keep their options open.
In 2031, there will be a new president in the Oval Office, a new governor, and a different political landscape in California — especially if voters approve Proposition 40 to impose a wealth tax that could prompt an exodus of the taxpayers targeted by Proposition 3.
Related Reading
CommentaryProposition 3 would help lock in hard-won resources for student well-being (https://edsource.org/2026/proposition-3-california-schools/769155) October 28, 2026
The state also will have significantly fewer students in our public schools. The Department of Finance projects a decline of 710,500 students from 2026 through 2036, and by the midpoint of this decline, we undoubtedly will see some major changes in the education structure.
This is only the beginning of the list of unknowns. Other questions include:
Will Californians still be paying billions of dollars per year for a nonfunctioning “high-speed” railroad system in 2031, rather than prioritizing schools for that spending?
Will taxpayers still be paying for ineffective programs that haven’t solved homelessness?
Will startups launch in California, or take their jobs and economic benefits to states with more competitive tax rates?
In short, it makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
What difference could five years make?
California’s finances can change substantially in a short period. Total state revenue for the current fiscal year is projected to be $21.5 billion higher than the amount collected five years earlier. The Department of Finance also recently reported that general fund revenue was running $5.5 billion above the projection used to draft the 2026-27 budget just six months earlier. This means the education funding guarantee will go up, too.
It makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
Timing is only one of the problems. While Proposition 3 is marketed as a “tax extension” that would only affect high-income residents, the truth is that it’s a major tax increase that would hit millions of small businesses as well as high-income individuals. The result: California’s affordability crisis gets worse.
The small-business aspect of Proposition 3 hasn’t received enough attention. California’s tax structure does not neatly separate business income from personal income, and many small businesses operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships, or S corporations that report business earnings on personal income tax returns.
This means the higher tax rates imposed by Proposition 3 would increase taxes on many small businesses, ultimately leading to higher prices for customers, fewer job opportunities for workers, or both.
ThePublic Policy Institute of California reported in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-businesses/) that sole proprietorships accounted for more than 3 million California businesses in 2023. But the number of those businesses whose owners would be impacted by Proposition 3 depends on their taxable income.
To the extent that Proposition 3 would hit high-income earners, it would make California more reliant on the most volatile source of revenue, while simultaneously making it even more volatile by giving high-income residents a new incentive to leave the state.
California already imposes the nation’s highest personal income taxes and would have a top personal income tax rate of 10.3% on income over $1 million without Proposition 3. The state also imposes a 1.3% State Disability Insurance tax on all income from salaries and wages, bringing the top tax rate to 11.6% on those forms of income, without Proposition 3.
As for the issue of an “extension” versus an “increase,” the fact is clear: If Proposition 3 is approved, Californians will pay $5 billion to $15 billion a year more in state income tax than if the initiative is defeated (according to estimates by the Legislative Analyst’s Office). That’s an increase — and a very large one, at that.
Finally, the measure would continue the trend in which “temporary” taxes in California never seem to go away. As the proponents of Proposition 40 are discovering, voters are extremely distrustful of taxes described as temporary. Why? In large part because of Proposition 3 and its predecessor, Proposition 55 of 2016, asking voters to renew a tax originally described as a temporary charge to cover an emergency.
The ballot argument for the original initiative, Proposition 30 of 2012, said the taxes “are temporary, balanced and necessary to protect schools and safety” — one of the argument’s five mentions of the allegedly temporary nature.
With revenue arriving above projections and the state spending billions on questionable programs without proper controls or a review of effectiveness, it can no longer be said that California has a fiscal emergency.
The voters should give much-needed relief to small businesses and their customers, avoid making fiscal decisions prematurely, and let the “emergency tax” expire on schedule. Vote NO on Proposition 3.

Prop
3

Constitutional Amendment
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes
Makes permanent the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners to fund education, healthcare, and other state programs.
SPUR's Recommendation
Prop. 3 would make permanent an existing high-earner tax that funds K–12/community college education, children’s healthcare, and debt paydown. This tax has generated more than $119 billion for education and healthcare, with no evidence that it has driven high earners out of state. It’s highly progressive, hitting only top earners while sustaining programs such as universal school meals that disproportionately benefit low-income students, and it would help backfill Medi-Cal funding just as federal cuts threaten healthcare access for millions of low-income Californians. The trade-offs are modest: permanence would limit future tax flexibility, and reliance on capital-gains-linked income would keep revenue volatile. But given the tax's proven track record and the increasingly dramatic funding gaps the tax would help fill in the wake of H.R. 1, SPUR supports making it permanent.
Vote YES
What Prop. 3 Would Do
Proposition 3 would amend the California Constitution to permanently extend the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners, which have been in place since 2012 under Proposition 55 and are set to expire in 2030. In 2025, the top 2% income bracket started at $371,001 a year for individuals and $743,001 a year for couples filing jointly. The tax applies to salaries, wages, interest, and profits from stocks, property, and other investments.
Revenue would primarily support K–12 schools and community colleges under 1988’s Proposition 98. About 40% — $2 billion to $6 billion annually — would go to education, while remaining funds could support children’s healthcare, the Budget Stabilization Account (rainy day fund), and other General Fund uses. Because the revenue counts toward the state’s required education funding, it frees up General Fund dollars for other programs. 1
If the tax rates set in 2012 expire, the state would lose between $5 billion and $15 billion annually. 2 In the short term, the state would need other General Fund revenues to meet education funding requirements; over time, the Proposition 98-mandated spending minimum could decline depending on the formula in use, economic conditions, and legislative decisions.
The Backstory
California’s personal income tax structure is the most progressive in the country (meaning the tax rate is higher the more income one earns). Voters approved Prop. 30 in 2012 to temporarily raise rates on high earners, then extended it through Prop. 55 in 2016 (expiring in 2030). Before Prop. 30, the top rate was 9.3%.
The tax structure for the top 2% of earners in California under different scenarios depends on whether Prop. 3 passes.

Constitutional Amendment
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes
Makes permanent the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners to fund education, healthcare, and other state programs.
SPUR's Recommendation
Prop. 3 would make permanent an existing high-earner tax that funds K–12/community college education, children’s healthcare, and debt paydown. This tax has generated more than $119 billion for education and healthcare, with no evidence that it has driven high earners out of state. It’s highly progressive, hitting only top earners while sustaining programs such as universal school meals that disproportionately benefit low-income students, and it would help backfill Medi-Cal funding just as federal cuts threaten healthcare access for millions of low-income Californians. The trade-offs are modest: permanence would limit future tax flexibility, and reliance on capital-gains-linked income would keep revenue volatile. But given the tax's proven track record and the increasingly dramatic funding gaps the tax would help fill in the wake of H.R. 1, SPUR supports making it permanent.
Vote YES
What Prop. 3 Would Do
Proposition 3 would amend the California Constitution to permanently extend the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners, which have been in place since 2012 under Proposition 55 and are set to expire in 2030. In 2025, the top 2% income bracket started at $371,001 a year for individuals and $743,001 a year for couples filing jointly. The tax applies to salaries, wages, interest, and profits from stocks, property, and other investments.
