In summary
California voters haven’t had to make so many decisions about tax policy at the ballot since 1990. Our analysis shows voters tend to reject new taxes.
Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State.
California voters will soon be asked whether they want to keep taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) the incomes of the rich.
And they’ll be asked whether to start taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) the accumulated wealth of the even richer.
Wait, there’s more. They’ll also get to weigh in on whether we should ban wealth taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) altogether, subject the money raised by future taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) to a state spending cap and make it harder for voters to pass certain local taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/).
That doesn’t include any of the other propositions on the November ballot that are likely to affect the state budget. Nor does it include the roughly 300 (https://www.caltax.org/elections/local-tax-elections/2026-Local-Elections.pdf?_gl=1*pjll0w*_ga*NTYyOTYwNzgyLjE3NzYyODUwNTE.*_ga_RR9B893WL0*czE3OTA3MjI1MTEkbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGo0MyRsMCRoMA..*_ga_98RV0P0X7N*czE3OTA3MjI1MDckbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGozOSRsMCRoMA..) tax and bond measures that will be popping up in local elections across the state.
And you thought tax season only came in April.
With 14 measures in total, the 2026 California ballot (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) is a busy one. Voters haven’t been presented with this many choices in a decade. It’s an especially active year for tax-related measures — those that hike taxes, cut them, introduce new ones, jettison old ones or change the rules by which taxes are approved and enacted.
Five of those are on the ballot this time around, the most since 1990.
Altogether they have the potential to reshape the state’s finances, beef up or starve some of our largest public spending programs, change the rules around taxation and — if opponents of the proposed wealth tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) are to be believed — trigger a Randian exodus of the state’s wellest-to-do.
The ‘black hole’ on the ballot
Though five tax measures are on the ballot, voters are really just seeing three big questions.
The first: Should California be the first state in the nation to introduce a wealth tax?
That question is “the black hole into which all political energy is going right now,” said Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a group that advocates for low taxes.

Three measures — Propositions 40, 41 and 42 — provide opposing answers.
Prop. 40 would slap every Californian with a net worth of at least $1 billion (all approximately 200 of them) with a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, excluding real estate and retirement accounts.
This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
A sign displayed at the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco on Feb. 21, 2026. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).
For the record: An earlier version of this article misstated the last time voters were presented with five or more tax-related measures on the same California ballot. The most recent year was 1990, not 1994.

The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.

Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.

And they’ll be asked whether to start taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) the accumulated wealth of the even richer.
Wait, there’s more. They’ll also get to weigh in on whether we should ban wealth taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) altogether, subject the money raised by future taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) to a state spending cap and make it harder for voters to pass certain local taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/).

And you thought tax season only came in April.

I'm noting the key points from this CalMatters piece: the Prop 40 wealth tax, with Props 41 and 42 as countermeasures where the higher vote tally wins if more than one passes. Prop 3 has 58% support per PPIC, and since 2000 non-tax measures have passed at a much higher rate (57%) than tax propositions (about a third), which is a useful base rate.

I'm weighing how the Prop 3 conflict clause applies here: it targets measures affecting personal income tax rates, and the wealth tax in Prop 40 isn't one, so it likely doesn't trigger. I'm also noting that voter support for propositions tends to slip as Election Day nears, and that Baldassare's point about the status quo being a safe bet when voters are unsure is relevant.

I'm dropping the detail about Prop 3's conflicting-measures clause, since none of the other measures on the ballot seem to touch personal income tax rates. I'm also noting that Prop 3's supporters, like the CTA, are focusing on Prop 3 rather than campaigning against Prop 40, while some proponents worry Prop 40 could undermine Prop 3.

I'm weighing whether to give a flat yes or no on this measure, since that would mean taking a side on a value-laden ballot question. Refusing outright seems off too, so I'll lay out what the evidence supports and let the user decide quickly.

I'm checking whether either side's factual claims are clearly wrong. The No side's "largest permanent tax increase" line isn't verifiable from what I have, but the "$100 billion surplus into a deficit" figure roughly matches reported numbers, even if the framing about causes is partisan.

I'm checking the Yes side's claim that Prop 3 "does NOT raise taxes on anyone." That holds for current law, but the rates would otherwise expire around 2031, so making them permanent is still a tax increase relative to that baseline. Both framings contain some truth, and the LAO describes it as a temporary tax increase made permanent.

I'm checking the Yes side's claim against the LAO's wording: the measure keeps current rates from expiring in 2031, so whether it counts as a "tax increase" depends on the baseline. Relative to today's rates it changes nothing, but relative to the 2031 expiration it keeps taxes several billion dollars a year higher, so both framings hold some truth.

I'm checking the Yes side's claim that every dollar goes to classrooms against the LAO's figure of about 40% going to schools and colleges, which makes that phrasing look misleading as a description of the whole measure. Their point that the schools guarantee frees up money for Medi-Cal is a separate claim I'll need to weigh on its own.

I'm checking the Yes side's school-funding framing against the LAO's estimate that about 40% of the revenue goes to schools and colleges. The "without Prop. 3, students face cuts" line is a forecast that depends on how the state responds, and the CTA's 50,000 layoff figure is their own estimate. I'm also looking at the No side's claim that Californians already pay the nation's highest income, sales, and gas taxes, since that's a ranking I'd need to verify.

I'm checking the No side's ranking claims: California's top 13.3% income tax rate does look like the highest in the country, and its combined sales and gas taxes are among the highest, though exact rankings shift with local rates and which taxes count. I'm also looking at the SPUR claim about out-migration, which says there's no evidence high earners left because of the tax.

I'm checking whether the out-migration argument holds up: the pro side points to a doubling of high-income filers since 2013, while the No side warns of wealthy residents leaving, and the research on state tax changes and interstate moves looks mixed but leans toward small effects.

I'm wondering whether the out-migration question has real evidence behind it. The research on tax-driven moves by high earners looks like it shows a modest effect overall, with the top sliver more sensitive, so I'm considering a quick search for a study on Prop 30 and migration to pin that down.

The wealth tax's volatility is another point both sides accept: the LAO estimates it would swing by roughly $5 to $15 billion a year depending on the stock market. Both sides also agree that enshrining the rates in the Constitution would require voter approval to change, so the real question is stability versus flexibility. That leaves the disputes over facts as moderate, with the main issue being a values trade-off over whether to keep taxing the top 2% at current rates rather than letting them fall back to 9.3% in 2031.

The base rates look relevant here: tax measures tend to pass less often than other propositions, while framing it as a renewal polls better. I'll keep that as context rather than a deciding factor, and note that voters who are unsure tend to default to no. Next I want to check the research on whether high earners actually leave California because of this kind of tax, since that claim is central to the No side's case.

I'm noting the key points from this CalMatters piece: the Prop 40 wealth tax, with Props 41 and 42 as countermeasures where the higher vote tally wins if more than one passes. Prop 3 has 58% support per PPIC, and since 2000 non-tax measures have passed at a much higher rate (57%) than tax propositions (about a third), which is a useful base rate.

I'm weighing how the Prop 3 conflict clause applies here: it targets measures affecting personal income tax rates, and the wealth tax in Prop 40 isn't one, so it likely doesn't trigger. I'm also noting that voter support for propositions tends to slip as Election Day nears, and that Baldassare's point about the status quo being a safe bet when voters are unsure is relevant.

I'm dropping the detail about Prop 3's conflicting-measures clause, since none of the other measures on the ballot seem to touch personal income tax rates. I'm also noting that Prop 3's supporters, like the CTA, are focusing on Prop 3 rather than campaigning against Prop 40, while some proponents worry Prop 40 could undermine Prop 3.

I'm weighing whether to give a flat yes or no on this measure, since that would mean taking a side on a value-laden ballot question. Refusing outright seems off too, so I'll lay out what the evidence supports and let the user decide quickly.

I'm checking whether either side's factual claims are clearly wrong. The No side's "largest permanent tax increase" line isn't verifiable from what I have, but the "$100 billion surplus into a deficit" figure roughly matches reported numbers, even if the framing about causes is partisan.

I'm checking the Yes side's claim that Prop 3 "does NOT raise taxes on anyone." That holds for current law, but the rates would otherwise expire around 2031, so making them permanent is still a tax increase relative to that baseline. Both framings contain some truth, and the LAO describes it as a temporary tax increase made permanent.

I'm checking the Yes side's claim against the LAO's wording: the measure keeps current rates from expiring in 2031, so whether it counts as a "tax increase" depends on the baseline. Relative to today's rates it changes nothing, but relative to the 2031 expiration it keeps taxes several billion dollars a year higher, so both framings hold some truth.

I'm checking the Yes side's claim that every dollar goes to classrooms against the LAO's figure of about 40% going to schools and colleges, which makes that phrasing look misleading as a description of the whole measure. Their point that the schools guarantee frees up money for Medi-Cal is a separate claim I'll need to weigh on its own.

I'm checking the Yes side's school-funding framing against the LAO's estimate that about 40% of the revenue goes to schools and colleges. The "without Prop. 3, students face cuts" line is a forecast that depends on how the state responds, and the CTA's 50,000 layoff figure is their own estimate. I'm also looking at the No side's claim that Californians already pay the nation's highest income, sales, and gas taxes, since that's a ranking I'd need to verify.

I'm checking the No side's ranking claims: California's top 13.3% income tax rate does look like the highest in the country, and its combined sales and gas taxes are among the highest, though exact rankings shift with local rates and which taxes count. I'm also looking at the SPUR claim about out-migration, which says there's no evidence high earners left because of the tax.

I'm checking whether the out-migration argument holds up: the pro side points to a doubling of high-income filers since 2013, while the No side warns of wealthy residents leaving, and the research on state tax changes and interstate moves looks mixed but leans toward small effects.

I'm wondering whether the out-migration question has real evidence behind it. The research on tax-driven moves by high earners looks like it shows a modest effect overall, with the top sliver more sensitive, so I'm considering a quick search for a study on Prop 30 and migration to pin that down.

The wealth tax's volatility is another point both sides accept: the LAO estimates it would swing by roughly $5 to $15 billion a year depending on the stock market. Both sides also agree that enshrining the rates in the Constitution would require voter approval to change, so the real question is stability versus flexibility. That leaves the disputes over facts as moderate, with the main issue being a values trade-off over whether to keep taxing the top 2% at current rates rather than letting them fall back to 9.3% in 2031.

The base rates look relevant here: tax measures tend to pass less often than other propositions, while framing it as a renewal polls better. I'll keep that as context rather than a deciding factor, and note that voters who are unsure tend to default to no. Next I want to check the research on whether high earners actually leave California because of this kind of tax, since that claim is central to the No side's case.

I won't give a one-word pick on this one. It turns on values: how much to weigh school and health funding against taxes on the top 2%, and whether to lock the rate in now. Here's what the research shows so you can decide.

**Facts both sides accept**
- **Yes** makes the top state rates permanent: 10.3–12.3% on income above roughly $371K (single) or $743K (joint), or 13.3% with the 1% mental-health surcharge, the nation's highest. **No** lets them expire in 2031, when the top rate falls to 9.3%.
- The Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) estimates the tax brings in $5–15 billion a year. That amount is volatile because it tracks the stock market. The top 2% already pay about half of state income tax.
- About 40% goes to K-14 schools (89% K-12, 11% community colleges). The rest goes to other state programs and reserves, including up to $2 billion a year for children's health care. The yes campaign acknowledges that the freed-up money goes to Medi-Cal.
- It would be written into the constitution, so later changes would generally need voter approval.
- The state faces deficits. The LAO projects $20–30 billion a year in structural shortfalls and notes General Fund spending has risen about $100 billion since 2019–20.

**Where the disagreement is**
- **"Tax increase" or not?** It doesn't raise current rates. Compared with 2031, it keeps $5–15 billion a year that would otherwise disappear. Both labels are defensible, depending on the baseline.
- **Do high earners leave?** Stanford/Hoover economist Joshua Rauh found that departures and income shifts after Prop 30 erased almost half the expected revenue gain. Other researchers found only a "very slight difference" in migration, and Rauh argues they undercounted movers. It's unresolved.
- **Spending vs. revenue:** Opponents say the state should fix spending first. Supporters say cuts would hit schools and Medi-Cal without this money.
- **Small business:** Opponents say many pass-through businesses report income on personal returns and would be hit too. Supporters say the tax applies only to the top 2%.

**The decision turns on**
1. Would losing $5–15 billion a year from 2031 hurt programs you care about more than keeping the top rate costs high earners?
2. Do you expect high earners' responses to shrink the revenue more than estimated?
3. Are you comfortable locking this in five years before it expires?

Sources: [LAO analysis](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026), [official voter guide](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/), [CalMatters](https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/), [Stanford GSB on Rauh and Shyu](https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/insights/has-california-hit-limit-tax-rates).

content.text:
I won't give a one-word pick on this one. It turns on values: how much to weigh school and health funding against taxes on the top 2%, and whether to lock the rate in now. Here's what the research shows so you can decide.

**Facts both sides accept**
- **Yes** makes the top state rates permanent: 10.3–12.3% on income above roughly $371K (single) or $743K (joint), or 13.3% with the 1% mental-health surcharge, the nation's highest. **No** lets them expire in 2031, when the top rate falls to 9.3%.
- The Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) estimates the tax brings in $5–15 billion a year. That amount is volatile because it tracks the stock market. The top 2% already pay about half of state income tax.
- About 40% goes to K-14 schools (89% K-12, 11% community colleges). The rest goes to other state programs and reserves, including up to $2 billion a year for children's health care. The yes campaign acknowledges that the freed-up money goes to Medi-Cal.
- It would be written into the constitution, so later changes would generally need voter approval.
- The state faces deficits. The LAO projects $20–30 billion a year in structural shortfalls and notes General Fund spending has risen about $100 billion since 2019–20.

**Where the disagreement is**
- **"Tax increase" or not?** It doesn't raise current rates. Compared with 2031, it keeps $5–15 billion a year that would otherwise disappear. Both labels are defensible, depending on the baseline.
- **Do high earners leave?** Stanford/Hoover economist Joshua Rauh found that departures and income shifts after Prop 30 erased almost half the expected revenue gain. Other researchers found only a "very slight difference" in migration, and Rauh argues they undercounted movers. It's unresolved.
- **Spending vs. revenue:** Opponents say the state should fix spending first. Supporters say cuts would hit schools and Medi-Cal without this money.
- **Small business:** Opponents say many pass-through businesses report income on personal returns and would be hit too. Supporters say the tax applies only to the top 2%.

**The decision turns on**
1. Would losing $5–15 billion a year from 2031 hurt programs you care about more than keeping the top rate costs high earners?
2. Do you expect high earners' responses to shrink the revenue more than estimated?
3. Are you comfortable locking this in five years before it expires?

Sources: [LAO analysis](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026), [official voter guide](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/), [CalMatters](https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/), [Stanford GSB on Rauh and Shyu](https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/insights/has-california-hit-limit-tax-rates).

I won't give a one-word pick on this one. It turns on values: how much to weigh school and health funding against taxes on the top 2%, and whether to lock the rate in now. Here's what the research shows so you can decide.

**Facts both sides accept**
- **Yes** makes the top state rates permanent: 10.3–12.3% on income above roughly $371K (single) or $743K (joint), or 13.3% with the 1% mental-health surcharge, the nation's highest. **No** lets them expire in 2031, when the top rate falls to 9.3%.
- The Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) estimates the tax brings in $5–15 billion a year. That amount is volatile because it tracks the stock market. The top 2% already pay about half of state income tax.
- About 40% goes to K-14 schools (89% K-12, 11% community colleges). The rest goes to other state programs and reserves, including up to $2 billion a year for children's health care. The yes campaign acknowledges that the freed-up money goes to Medi-Cal.
- It would be written into the constitution, so later changes would generally need voter approval.
- The state faces deficits. The LAO projects $20–30 billion a year in structural shortfalls and notes General Fund spending has risen about $100 billion since 2019–20.

**Where the disagreement is**
- **"Tax increase" or not?** It doesn't raise current rates. Compared with 2031, it keeps $5–15 billion a year that would otherwise disappear. Both labels are defensible, depending on the baseline.
- **Do high earners leave?** Stanford/Hoover economist Joshua Rauh found that departures and income shifts after Prop 30 erased almost half the expected revenue gain. Other researchers found only a "very slight difference" in migration, and Rauh argues they undercounted movers. It's unresolved.
- **Spending vs. revenue:** Opponents say the state should fix spending first. Supporters say cuts would hit schools and Medi-Cal without this money.
- **Small business:** Opponents say many pass-through businesses report income on personal returns and would be hit too. Supporters say the tax applies only to the top 2%.

**The decision turns on**
1. Would losing $5–15 billion a year from 2031 hurt programs you care about more than keeping the top rate costs high earners?
2. Do you expect high earners' responses to shrink the revenue more than estimated?
3. Are you comfortable locking this in five years before it expires?

Sources: [LAO analysis](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026), [official voter guide](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/), [CalMatters](https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/), [Stanford GSB on Rauh and Shyu](https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/insights/has-california-hit-limit-tax-rates).

3
PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It pays for most spending from the state’s main operating account, the General Fund. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000 and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
PROPOSAL
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market, which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.

PROP. 3 PREVENTS BILLIONS IN CUTS TO OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE.
Without Prop. 3, California’s 8 million public school and community college students face billions in cuts, including teacher layoffs, overcrowded classrooms and bigger class sizes. Families could lose access to preventive healthcare and affordable prescription drugs, and the Medi-Cal coverage that millions of Californians rely on could be put at risk.
PROP. 3 ONLY EXTENDS THE CURRENT TAX RATES ON THE WEALTHIEST TOP 2%.
Prop. 3 maintains the income tax rates that the wealthiest Californians have paid for the past 15 years. If those tax rates are allowed to expire, it would give millionaires and billionaires a massive tax cut at the expense of our classrooms, clinics and communities. Proposition 3 keeps the existing rates on the top 2% of incomes.
GUARANTEES THE MONEY REACHES THE CLASSROOM— NOT SACRAMENTO.
Proposition 3 includes Constitutional protections and tough accountability. It guarantees that funds from Proposition 3 go directly to local schools—the Legislature and Sacramento politicians cannot touch it, redirect it, or spend a single dollar on bureaucracy or administrative overhead. Prop. 3’s school guarantee then frees up billions that help fund Medi-Cal for children, seniors and families.
Every dollar in Prop. 3 is independently audited every year and any official who misuses the money faces prosecution and criminal penalties. Local school districts must post annual accounting online to guarantee that Californians know exactly how and where funds are spent.
PROP. 3 SECURES OUR CHILDREN’S FUTURE.
For more than a decade, these revenues have helped fund critical programs California families and communities count on—from school lunches, smaller class sizes and mental health counselors to children’s healthcare and Medi-Cal. They’ve also helped stave off cuts during economic downturns by investing more in the state’s Rainy Day Fund, protecting our schools and healthcare when the economy slows. Proposition 3 keeps that progress going for the next generation.
PROP. 3 IS SUPPORTED BY TEACHERS, NURSES, AND HEALTHCARE WORKERS.
Yes on 3 is supported by:
California State PTA
California Federation of Teachers
California Nurses Association
California School Employees Association
California School Nurses Organization
California Teachers Association
Community College League of California
Nurse Alliance of SEIU California
Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA
The educators in our classrooms and the nurses who care for our kids all agree: Vote YES on Proposition 3. Let’s protect what matters most, without raising your taxes. Vote YES on Proposition 3.
www.YesProp3CA.com
David Goldberg , President
California Teachers Association
Katie Nilsson , RN, President
California School Nurses Organization
Jodi Hicks , President
Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 3
NO ON PROP. 3—STOP PERMANENTLY HIGHER INCOME TAXES
In 2012, politicians and special interests promised Californians that their income tax increases would be TEMPORARY. Now they’re claiming that making those taxes permanent somehow ISN’T a tax increase at all. Don’t buy it. Prop. 3 locks in what would become the largest permanent state income tax increase in California history— costing taxpayers up to $15 billion every year.
NO ON PROP. 3—REMIND POLITICIANS WHAT “TEMPORARY” MEANS
Temporary: lasting for a limited time only; not permanent.
California taxpayers kept their end of the bargain—paying temporary higher income taxes for 16 years. Politicians should keep theirs and stop pushing for even higher taxes.
NO ON PROP. 3—STOP WASTEFUL SPENDING
Prop. 3 does nothing to stop the waste, fraud and reckless spending that turned a $100 billion budget surplus into a $30 billion deficit in just three years. If Sacramento had spent responsibly, they wouldn’t be asking taxpayers to make “temporary” taxes permanent.
NO ON PROP. 3—DON’T MAKE CALIFORNIA EVEN MORE EXPENSIVE
Californians have the highest cost of living and pay the highest income, sales and gas taxes in America. Making a temporary tax permanent only makes California more expensive.
NO ON PROP. 3—FIX THE SPENDING PROBLEM FIRST
California doesn’t have a tax revenue problem—it has a spending problem. California’s population grew by less than 2% in the past decade while the politicians doubled spending. Say no to permanently higher taxes. Join us to oppose higher income taxes at VoteNoProp3.com .
NO ON PROP. 3

ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 3
PROP. 3-TURNS "TEMPORARY" TAXES INTO PERMANENT HIGHER INCOME TAXES
Sacramento politicians make big promises to get our support for higher taxes. Then they spend our tax dollars with no accountability-losing billions to waste, fraud and overspending.
Take Prop. 3. Politicians told voters higher income taxes would be temporary-only for seven years to cover a budget deficit. Then those "temporary" taxes were extended for another 12 years with the promise to voters that the higher taxes would solve the problems the politicians created. Now the special interests and politicians want to make these higher income taxes PERMANENT.
California voters should say NO to PERMANENTLY higher income taxes.
PROP. 3-HIGHER INCOME TAXES = HIGHER COST OF LIVING
Californians have the nation's highest cost of living partly because we also suffer from the highest income taxes, highest sales taxes and highest gas taxes of all fifty states. The same politicians also gave us the highest gasoline prices in the nation, higher insurance costs, higher utility costs, higher food costs, and higher housing costs. Now they want to make higher income taxes permanent, while adding new taxes on your health insurance, new taxes on software-and they are even considering a "jobs" tax. Say NO to INCREASING our cost of living with higher taxes.
PROP. 3-VOTERS DESERVE REAL RESULTS, NOT BROKEN PROMISES
Waste, fraud and overspending by state government is not an excuse to raise our taxes even higher.
The politicians and special interests promised temporary income taxes were needed to avoid big cuts to government programs. Since the "temporary" increases were first passed, government spending has increased by $150 billion-a more than 2.5X increase. Over the same time period, our schools, infrastructure and public safety have gotten worse. Say NO to endless broken promises.
NO ON PROP. 3-STOP WASTEFUL SPENDING
The politicians and special interests turned a $100 billion budget surplus into a $30 billion budget deficit in just three years. They mismanaged our tax dollars so badly, they now want voters to bail them out with permanently higher taxes.
Say NO to $100 billion wasted on a train to nowhere.
Say NO to $37 billion wasted on homeless programs that don't work.
Say NO to $31 billion wasted on unemployment fraud.
NO ON PROP. 3-FIX SACRAMENTO'S SPENDING PROBLEM BEFORE RAISING TAXES
California doesn't have a revenue problem. We have a spending problem. California's population barely grew in the past 10 years, but the politicians more than doubled spending.
It's not just state taxes that keep going up. Politicians and special interests have imposed more than 2,000 new local tax increases in just the past ten years-making it much harder for struggling Californians to make ends meet.
Californians shouldn't support any higher taxes until we get spending under control.
STOP WASTEFUL SPENDING.
NO NEW TAXES.
NO ON PROP. 3.

PROPOSITION 3
Proposition 3 protects our schools, our healthcare and our communities—without raising your taxes.
PROP. 3 KEEPS THE TAX RATES THE TOP 2% HAVE PAID FOR THE PAST 15 YEARS AND DOES NOT RAISE YOUR TAXES.
Prop. 3 maintains the current tax rates the wealthiest 2% of Californians have been paying for 15 years, ensuring couples that earn more than $740,000 continue to pay their fair share.
WITHOUT PROP. 3 MILLIONAIRES AND BILLIONAIRES GET A MASSIVE TAX CUT—AND THE REST OF US PAY FOR IT.
Teacher and staff layoffs, overcrowded classrooms and fewer counselors in our schools; cuts to Medi-Cal, children’s healthcare and the clinics families rely on; and less for the firefighters, emergency response and wildfire protection that keep our communities safe.

Prop. 3’s funding goes straight to local schools and community colleges. Sacramento politicians cannot touch it or redirect it. Not one penny may be spent on bureaucracy or administrative overhead. Every dollar is independently audited every year, districts must post their spending online, and any official who misuses the money faces prosecution and criminal penalties.
PROP. 3 PROTECTS HEALTHCARE AND FIRE PROTECTION.

PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Makes permanent the existing 2012 voter-approved tax rates for high-income Californians, currently set to expire in 2031.
Rates apply to income over about $371,000 for single filers, $742,000 for joint filers, and $505,000 for heads of household (2025 levels; adjusted annually for inflation).
Allocates tax revenues 89% to K-12 schools, 11% to community colleges.
Allows local school boards to decide how revenues are spent; bars use for administrative costs.
Increases General Fund revenues available for health care, budget reserves, and other programs.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031.

## Proposition 3: Provides Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care By Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
### Additional Titles
High-Income Tax, Renew State Income Tax Increase for Education Funding Initiative
The California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026
### Summary
Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering.
874,641 valid signatures were required.
The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents.
These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 through 2030.
Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent.
Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets.
The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.

It would make permanent the existing tax rates, which are set to expire after 2030.
If passed, 89% of tax revenue will continue to fund K-12 schools and the remaining 11% will go to community colleges.
These increased tax rates were initially passed by voters in 2012 during a budget deficit, and were extended by voters in 2016.
Each year, the high-income tax rates bring in between $5 billion and $15 billion for the state, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office.
The revenue has ranged year to year depending on earnings from the stock market and other outside factors.
For those who earn over $1 million, that tax has been on top of another existing 1% tax that goes toward mental health services.
David Goldberg, the president of the California Teachers Association, which supports the proposition, told CalMatters that if the measure doesn't pass, about 50,000 teachers could be laid off.
The ballot measure also has support from the National Education Association and the California School Employees Association.

If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last. Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031. “I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.” Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners. READ NEXT Billionaire tax, affordable housing: See the measures on California’s November ballot (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-ballot-measures-november-election/) June 25, 2026 June 30, 2026 Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2024/02/california-mental-health-history/) and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3% (https://taxfoundation.org/location/california/), the highest in the nation. The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges. In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said. Union’s big push The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.” The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500. The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) on the measure. Among Democrats, 82% said they favored it, while 18% of Republicans said they did. Proposition 40 would levy a 5% tax on Californians with assets of more than $1 billion, with 90% of the money going toward healthcare and the rest divided between schools, food assistance programs and other services. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said. “We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said. The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said. ‘Not sustainable’ Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/05/california-schools-funding-increases/) and declining enrollment (https://calmatters.org/education/k-12-education/2024/11/school-closures/). “We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.” In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016), the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes. California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living. Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students (https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/tables/202223_summary_2.asp), according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11. That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now. “Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.” He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding. “No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said. What to know about California’s other tax-the-rich measure: Prop. 3

By Carolyn Jones, CalMatters

November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 3
PROPOSITION 3
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by
Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional
Amendment.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It
pays for most spending from the state’s main operating account, the General Fund. The General
Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health
care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and
profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out
low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple
pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000
and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily
increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to
extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher
rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion
from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for
schools, community colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a
minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state
spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health
insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 3
PROPOSAL
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent
instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this
measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount
of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is
because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market,
which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in
revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the
state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education
and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community
colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in
budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 3 of 3
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place
since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
A NO vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place
since 2012 would expire in 2031.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a
temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in
2031.

Fiscal Impact: Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by
making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in
2031.

ers.

If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last.

Prop. 3 would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031.

“I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.”

Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners. 

Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3%, the highest in the nation.

The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. 

Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges.

In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said.

Union’s big push

The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.”

The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500.

The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes on the measure. Among Democrats, 82% said they favored it, while 18% of Republicans said they did.

Prop. 3 is not the only tax-the-rich measure on the Nov. 3 ballot. Proposition 40 would levy a 5% tax on Californians with assets of more than $1 billion, with 90% of the money going toward healthcare and the rest divided between schools, food assistance programs and other services. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said. 

“We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said.

The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said.

‘Not sustainable’

Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments and declining enrollment. 

“We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.”

In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes. 

California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living.

Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11.

That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now. 

“Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.”

He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding.

“No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 3 would make an expiring state income tax on high earners permanent, which supporters say is critical to funding schools and healthcare.

Oct. 1, 2026
What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 3 stems from a decision voters made in 2012, amid a budget crisis, to temporarily increase the income tax rate on the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030.
Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
If passed, tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers.
Advertisement
If rejected, tax rates for the top 2% would fall in 2031 from at least 10.3% to 9.3%.
How much they have raised
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text">
Fundraising data will be updated regularly until the election.
What does the tax fund?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Then, because the state constitution requires minimum levels of spending on education, more dollars are freed up to pay for services including healthcare and the University of California and California State University systems, said Kayla Kitson, a senior analyst with the California Budget and Policy Center.
Proposition 3, like the current high-earners tax, has the added effect of raising the minimum levels of funding required to flow to K-12 schools and community colleges, because of the complicated formulas California uses to set its budget, Kitson said.
If Proposition 3 fails, the state could expect to lose between $5 billion and $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Advertisement
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Supporters of the measure include the California Teachers Assn., the California School Nurses Organization, the California State PTA and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California.
The California Teachers Assn., whose members gathered signatures to put Proposition 3 on the ballot, says if voters reject the measure, public schools could face a 15% budget cut, with 1 in 6 educators at risk of losing their jobs.
“Prop. 3 keeps the wealthiest Californians paying their share so our public schools get the funding our students deserve,” the union says on its website (https://www.cta.org/educator/posts/yes-on-prop3).
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The California Taxpayers Assn., the Family Business Assn. of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce have come out against the measure.
Opponents say the state already has the nation’s highest income, sales and gas taxes and Sacramento needs to stop wasteful spending, rather than make taxes that were supposed to be temporary permanent.
Advertisement
“Californians shouldn’t have to bail out politicians and special interests’ mismanagement,” an opposition website sponsored by the California Taxpayers Assn. says. “Waste, fraud and overspending by the state government is not an excuse to raise our taxes even higher.”

Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Provides Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care By Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
High-Income Tax, Renew State Income Tax Increase for Education Funding Initiative
The California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering. 874,641 valid signatures were required. The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents. These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-6-2012-general-election-summary/november-6) in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-8-2016-general-election-summary/november-8-2) through 2030. Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent. Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets. The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 3 would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue that would otherwise disappear when the higher income tax rates expire after 2030. The amount collected would vary from year to year because earnings among high-income taxpayers are especially sensitive to changes in the economy and stock market. Roughly 40 percent of the additional revenue would support K–12 schools and community colleges, while most of the remainder would be available for other General Fund programs and state reserves.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote would permanently continue California’s higher income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% on high-income earners, with the resulting education funding divided between K–12 schools (89%) and community colleges (11%).
NO: A “no” vote would leave current law unchanged, allowing these higher tax rates to expire in 2031.

Proposition 3
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for most spending from the state's main operating account, the General Fund. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000 and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
Proposal
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
Fiscal Effects
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market, which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
A NO vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.

Story Title:
Proposition 3: California doesn’t need another forever tax
October 28, 2026
Download featured image (https://edsource.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/voting10.jpg)
This story was originally published by EdSource (https://edsource.org/2026/commentary-vote-no-proposition-3/769223). Sign up for their daily newsletter (https://edsource.org/subscribe).
Proposition 3 asks voters to approve a massive tax increase that would not take effect until 2031, when California’s finances may look completely different from how they do today. Voters should reject Proposition 3 and keep their options open.
In 2031, there will be a new president in the Oval Office, a new governor, and a different political landscape in California — especially if voters approve Proposition 40 to impose a wealth tax that could prompt an exodus of the taxpayers targeted by Proposition 3.
Related Reading
CommentaryProposition 3 would help lock in hard-won resources for student well-being (https://edsource.org/2026/proposition-3-california-schools/769155) October 28, 2026
The state also will have significantly fewer students in our public schools. The Department of Finance projects a decline of 710,500 students from 2026 through 2036, and by the midpoint of this decline, we undoubtedly will see some major changes in the education structure.
This is only the beginning of the list of unknowns. Other questions include:
Will Californians still be paying billions of dollars per year for a nonfunctioning “high-speed” railroad system in 2031, rather than prioritizing schools for that spending?
Will taxpayers still be paying for ineffective programs that haven’t solved homelessness?
Will startups launch in California, or take their jobs and economic benefits to states with more competitive tax rates?
In short, it makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
What difference could five years make?
California’s finances can change substantially in a short period. Total state revenue for the current fiscal year is projected to be $21.5 billion higher than the amount collected five years earlier. The Department of Finance also recently reported that general fund revenue was running $5.5 billion above the projection used to draft the 2026-27 budget just six months earlier. This means the education funding guarantee will go up, too.
It makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
Timing is only one of the problems. While Proposition 3 is marketed as a “tax extension” that would only affect high-income residents, the truth is that it’s a major tax increase that would hit millions of small businesses as well as high-income individuals. The result: California’s affordability crisis gets worse.
The small-business aspect of Proposition 3 hasn’t received enough attention. California’s tax structure does not neatly separate business income from personal income, and many small businesses operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships, or S corporations that report business earnings on personal income tax returns.
This means the higher tax rates imposed by Proposition 3 would increase taxes on many small businesses, ultimately leading to higher prices for customers, fewer job opportunities for workers, or both.
ThePublic Policy Institute of California reported in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-businesses/) that sole proprietorships accounted for more than 3 million California businesses in 2023. But the number of those businesses whose owners would be impacted by Proposition 3 depends on their taxable income.
To the extent that Proposition 3 would hit high-income earners, it would make California more reliant on the most volatile source of revenue, while simultaneously making it even more volatile by giving high-income residents a new incentive to leave the state.
California already imposes the nation’s highest personal income taxes and would have a top personal income tax rate of 10.3% on income over $1 million without Proposition 3. The state also imposes a 1.3% State Disability Insurance tax on all income from salaries and wages, bringing the top tax rate to 11.6% on those forms of income, without Proposition 3.
As for the issue of an “extension” versus an “increase,” the fact is clear: If Proposition 3 is approved, Californians will pay $5 billion to $15 billion a year more in state income tax than if the initiative is defeated (according to estimates by the Legislative Analyst’s Office). That’s an increase — and a very large one, at that.
Finally, the measure would continue the trend in which “temporary” taxes in California never seem to go away. As the proponents of Proposition 40 are discovering, voters are extremely distrustful of taxes described as temporary. Why? In large part because of Proposition 3 and its predecessor, Proposition 55 of 2016, asking voters to renew a tax originally described as a temporary charge to cover an emergency.
The ballot argument for the original initiative, Proposition 30 of 2012, said the taxes “are temporary, balanced and necessary to protect schools and safety” — one of the argument’s five mentions of the allegedly temporary nature.
With revenue arriving above projections and the state spending billions on questionable programs without proper controls or a review of effectiveness, it can no longer be said that California has a fiscal emergency.
The voters should give much-needed relief to small businesses and their customers, avoid making fiscal decisions prematurely, and let the “emergency tax” expire on schedule. Vote NO on Proposition 3.

Proposition 3 asks voters to approve a massive tax increase that would not take effect until 2031, when California’s finances may look completely different from how they do today. Voters should reject Proposition 3 and keep their options open.
In 2031, there will be a new president in the Oval Office, a new governor, and a different political landscape in California — especially if voters approve Proposition 40 to impose a wealth tax that could prompt an exodus of the taxpayers targeted by Proposition 3.
Related Reading
